stem: In an anesthetized animal, a fatty acid solution is infused into the duodenum. Twenty minutes later an intravenous glucose dose is given, and plasma glucose is cleared faster than when the same volume of normal saline was infused into the duodenum instead.
oneliner: Animal + duodenal fatty acids vs saline → faster plasma glucose clearance after IV glucose → which hormone?
ask: Which hormone most likely mediates this effect?

whyNot.A: Gastrin comes from **antral G cells** in response to peptides and distension, not **duodenal fat**, and drives acid, not insulin
whyNot.B: Motilin triggers **interdigestive motility**, not an effect on glucose disposal
whyNot.C: Fatty acids can release some secretin, but secretin drives **pancreatic bicarbonate**, not insulin, so it would not speed **glucose clearance**
whyNot.D: Somatostatin is **inhibitory**, lowering insulin, so glucose clearance would slow

why: Fat in the duodenum releases **GIP from K cells**. GIP **amplifies glucose-stimulated insulin secretion** from beta cells, so the same glucose load is cleared faster (the incretin effect).
chain: Fatty acids reach duodenal K cells
GIP is released
Beta cells are primed
Insulin response to glucose is larger
Plasma glucose is cleared faster

idea.rule: Nutrients in the gut release incretins (GIP, GLP-1) that amplify glucose-stimulated insulin release.
also: GLP-1 from L cells (target of GLP-1 agonists)
Oral glucose gives a larger insulin response than the same IV glucose
Gastric bypass raising GLP-1 after meals
DPP-4 inhibitors prolong incretin action

stem: A 50-year-old man has bronze-tinged skin and painful swelling of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. He has an enlarged liver. His brother has diabetes and cirrhosis. He does not drink alcohol and has never been transfused.
oneliner: 50M + bronze skin + 2nd-3rd MCP arthropathy + hepatomegaly + brother with diabetes and cirrhosis → which iron-study set?
ask: Which set of changes best fits his iron studies?

options.A: Serum iron ↓, ferritin ↑, TIBC ↓, transferrin saturation ↓
options.B: Serum iron ↓, ferritin ↓, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation ↓
options.C: Serum iron ↔, ferritin ↑, TIBC ↔, transferrin saturation ↔
options.D: Serum iron ↑, ferritin ↑, TIBC ↑, transferrin saturation ↑
options.E: Serum iron ↑, ferritin ↑, TIBC ↓, transferrin saturation ↑

whyNot.A: Iron-poor, ferritin-high is **anemia of chronic disease**; his iron stores are overloaded
whyNot.B: This is **iron deficiency**, the opposite of this multisystem iron deposition
whyNot.C: An isolated ferritin rise is an **acute-phase** response; skin, joint and liver deposition need high saturation
whyNot.D: Iron overload **saturates** transferrin and lowers TIBC; a high TIBC reflects low iron stores

answer: High iron, ferritin and saturation; low TIBC
why: Hereditary hemochromatosis (usually **HFE** C282Y) leaves **hepcidin** inappropriately low, so the gut absorbs too much iron. **Serum iron, ferritin and transferrin saturation rise**, while **TIBC falls** because the iron-loaded liver makes less transferrin.
chain: HFE mutation, low hepcidin
Excess intestinal iron absorption and ferroportin activity
Serum iron, ferritin, saturation up; TIBC down
Iron deposits in skin, joints, liver, pancreas, heart

idea.rule: Iron overload of any cause: iron, ferritin and saturation up, TIBC down.
also: Repeated transfusion in beta-thalassemia major or sickle cell disease
Ineffective erythropoiesis (beta-thalassemia intermedia) lowers hepcidin and raises absorption
Juvenile hemochromatosis from hemojuvelin or hepcidin gene mutations
Long-term excess oral or parenteral iron

stem: A 50-year-old man with long-standing chronic pancreatitis reports bulky, foul, floating stools, a steady loss of weight, dry scaly skin and difficulty seeing in dim light. Vitamin levels and a prothrombin time are sent.
oneliner: 50M + chronic pancreatitis + bulky floating stools + weight loss + dry scaly skin + poor night vision → vitamin A, vitamin D, PT, vitamin E?
ask: Which set of laboratory changes is expected?

options.A: Vitamin A ↓, vitamin D ↔, PT ↔, vitamin E ↔
options.B: Vitamin A ↓, vitamin D ↓, PT ↑, vitamin E ↓
options.C: Vitamin A ↔, vitamin D ↓, PT ↑, vitamin E ↓
options.D: Vitamin A ↓, vitamin D ↓, PT ↔, vitamin E ↓
options.E: Vitamin A ↔, vitamin D ↔, PT ↑, vitamin E ↔

whyNot.A: Only vitamin A falls here, yet his **bulky floating stools show fat malabsorption**, which drags down every fat-soluble vitamin, D, E and K included
whyNot.C: His **poor night vision and dry scaly skin** point to low vitamin A, so A cannot be normal
whyNot.D: Vitamin K is lost with the fat just like A, D and E, so with **fatty stools** the PT must lengthen
whyNot.E: Normal vitamin A does not fit his **night-vision trouble and dry scaly skin**, and D and E travel with the same unabsorbed fat

answer: Vitamin A, D and E fall and PT rises
why: Without lipase and bile-mixed micelles, **fat is not absorbed**, and the **fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K** travel with it into the stool. Low vitamin K lowers factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S), so the **prothrombin time lengthens**. Water-soluble vitamins are largely spared.
chain: Pancreatic lipase output falls
Dietary fat stays unabsorbed (steatorrhea)
Vitamins A, D and E are lost with the fat
Vitamin K deficiency lowers factors II, VII, IX, X
Night blindness, dry skin and a longer PT

idea.rule: Fat malabsorption removes all four fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K); water-soluble vitamins are largely spared.
also: Cholestasis (bile acids cannot reach the gut) gives the same pattern
Biliary atresia in infants causes fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, including vitamin E
Celiac disease and small-bowel Crohn disease
Orlistat and cholestyramine reduce fat-soluble vitamin absorption

stem: In a fasted anesthetized dog, a solution of fatty acids is infused into the first part of the duodenum with its pH kept neutral. Gallbladder pressure, sphincter of Oddi tone, pancreatic juice enzyme output and the rate of gastric emptying are recorded.
oneliner: Experiment + fatty acids into duodenum at neutral pH → gallbladder, sphincter of Oddi, pancreatic enzymes, gastric emptying?
ask: Which set of changes is expected?

options.A: Gallbladder relaxes, sphincter of Oddi contracts, enzymes ↑, gastric emptying faster
options.B: Gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi contracts, enzymes ↔, gastric emptying faster
options.C: Gallbladder ↔, sphincter of Oddi ↔, enzymes ↓, gastric emptying slower
options.D: Gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi relaxes, enzymes ↑, gastric emptying slower
options.E: Gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi relaxes, enzymes ↓, gastric emptying faster

whyNot.A: Fat in the duodenum calls for **bile release**, so the gallbladder must contract and the outlet must open, not the reverse
whyNot.B: A contracted outlet would **trap the bile** the gallbladder is pushing out; fat also needs enzymes, so output cannot stay flat
whyNot.C: No change in the biliary tract and falling enzymes would fit an **inhibitory** signal, but the stimulus here is **fat** needing digestion
whyNot.E: Digesting fat requires **more** lipase, not less, and faster emptying would flood the duodenum with more fat

answer: Gallbladder contracts, sphincter of Oddi relaxes, enzymes up, gastric emptying slows
why: Fatty acids and amino acids stimulate **I cells** to release **cholecystokinin**. CCK **contracts the gallbladder**, **relaxes the sphincter of Oddi**, raises **enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion** and **slows gastric emptying**, so the duodenum is not overloaded while fat is digested.
chain: Fat reaches the duodenum
I cells release CCK
Gallbladder contracts and Oddi relaxes
Acinar cells secrete enzymes
Gastric emptying slows to match digestion

idea.rule: CCK = fat and protein in the duodenum: bile out, enzymes out, stomach slows down.
also: Gallstone colic is worse after fatty meals as CCK makes the gallbladder contract
Amino acids and peptides in the duodenum release CCK the same way
CCK also signals satiety through vagal afferents
Somatostatinoma blocks CCK release: gallstones and steatorrhea

stem: An anesthetized dog has a fistula that collects pancreatic juice. Dilute hydrochloric acid is infused into the duodenum, and the volume, bicarbonate concentration and enzyme output of the juice are compared with the fasting baseline.
oneliner: Experiment + acid infused into duodenum + pancreatic fistula → juice volume, bicarbonate, enzymes?
ask: Which pattern of pancreatic juice is expected?

whyNot.B: Enzyme-rich juice with no extra fluid follows **fat or protein** in the duodenum; the infusion here is **acid**
whyNot.C: Everything falling is an **inhibitory** pattern; an **acid load** in the duodenum calls for neutralisation
whyNot.D: Acid needs **neutralising**, so bicarbonate must rise, not fall
whyNot.E: Secretin makes duct cells secrete **water along with bicarbonate**, so volume rises; enzyme output is the **acinar, fat-driven** response, not the acid one

answer: Large volume, bicarbonate-rich juice with little change in enzymes
why: Duodenal acid (pH below about 4.5) triggers **S cells** to release **secretin**. Secretin acts on pancreatic **duct cells** to produce a **large-volume, bicarbonate-rich** juice that neutralises acid, while enzyme output (an acinar, CCK-driven event) barely changes.
chain: Acid enters the duodenum
S cells release secretin
Duct cells secrete fluid and bicarbonate
Juice volume and bicarbonate rise
Acinar enzyme output stays near baseline

idea.rule: Secretin = acid in, bicarbonate out; CCK = fat in, enzymes out.
also: Secretin also lowers gastric acid secretion and gastrin release
Secretin makes bile-duct cells add bicarbonate-rich fluid to bile
Chronic pancreatitis loses bicarbonate, so duodenal pH stays low and lipase is inactivated
Secretin stimulation test checks pancreatic ductal function

stem: A 51-year-old woman has 6 months of burning epigastric pain that comes 2 to 3 hours after meals. Ulcers keep returning despite treatment, and a 2-cm mass is found in the duodenal wall. Serum gastrin is markedly raised and basal gastric acid output is high.
oneliner: 51F + recurrent ulcers + 2-cm duodenal mass + high gastrin + high basal acid → receptor and messenger the hormone itself uses?
ask: Which receptor and second messenger does the secreted hormone itself bind and activate on its target cells?

options.C: CCK-B receptor, Gq, IP3 and Ca2+ ↑

whyNot.A: H2 is the receptor for **histamine**, released downstream from ECL cells; the tumor itself secretes **gastrin**
whyNot.B: The secretin receptor binds **secretin**, which lowers acid; the tumor hormone here is **gastrin** and acid is **raised**
whyNot.D: Gi lowering cAMP is how **prostaglandin E2** reduces acid; the hormone here **raises** acid
whyNot.E: Guanylyl cyclase receptors bind natriuretic peptides and guanylin, not **gastrin**

answer: CCK-B receptor coupled to Gq, raising IP3 and calcium
why: Gastrin binds **CCK-B (CCK2) receptors** on parietal and ECL cells, which signal through **Gq, IP3 and Ca2+**. ECL cells release histamine, which adds **H2/Gs/cAMP** stimulation, so the parietal cell is driven by three pathways at once.
chain: Tumor releases gastrin continuously
Gastrin binds CCK-B receptors on ECL and parietal cells
Gq raises IP3 and intracellular Ca2+
ECL histamine adds H2/cAMP stimulation
Parietal acid output stays high, ulcers recur

idea.rule: Gastrin and ACh act through Gq (IP3/Ca2+); histamine acts through Gs (cAMP); prostaglandin E2 inhibits through Gi.
also: ACh from the vagus acts on M3 receptors (Gq, IP3/Ca2+) on parietal cells
CCK acts on CCK-A receptors, also Gq-coupled
H2 blockers cut the cAMP route; PPIs block the H+/K+ ATPase shared by all three
Misoprostol mimics the protective PGE2 (Gi) signal

stem: A 3-week-old girl is brought in with yellow skin for a week. Her mother says her stools have become pale clay in color and her urine stains the diaper dark. She is feeding well and is otherwise active.
oneliner: 3-week-old F + jaundice + pale stools + dark urine → conjugated bilirubin, urine bilirubin, urine urobilinogen, stool stercobilin?
ask: Which set of bilirubin findings is expected?

options.A: Conjugated bilirubin ↑, urine bilirubin ↑, urine urobilinogen ↑, stool stercobilin ↑
options.B: Conjugated bilirubin ↔, urine bilirubin ↔, urine urobilinogen ↑, stool stercobilin ↑
options.C: Conjugated bilirubin ↔, urine bilirubin ↔, urine urobilinogen ↔, stool stercobilin ↔
options.D: Conjugated bilirubin ↔, urine bilirubin ↑, urine urobilinogen ↓, stool stercobilin ↓
options.E: Conjugated bilirubin ↑, urine bilirubin ↑, urine urobilinogen ↓, stool stercobilin ↓

whyNot.A: Raised urobilinogen and stercobilin need bilirubin to **reach the gut**; her **pale stools** show it does not
whyNot.B: This is the hemolysis pattern: no bilirubin in urine fails to explain her **dark urine**, and more stercobilin would darken, not **pale**, the stool
whyNot.C: Unchanged pigments would leave stool and urine normal; she has **pale stools and dark urine**
whyNot.D: Bilirubin appears in urine only when the **conjugated fraction is raised**, so conjugated bilirubin cannot be normal with **dark urine**

answer: Conjugated bilirubin and urine bilirubin up; urine urobilinogen and stool stercobilin down
why: Conjugated bilirubin that cannot reach the intestine backs up into blood, and being water-soluble it spills into urine (**dark urine**). Without bilirubin in the gut, bacteria make **no urobilinogen**, so urinary urobilinogen and **stool stercobilin fall** and stools turn **pale**.
chain: Bile flow to the duodenum is blocked
Conjugated bilirubin regurgitates into blood
Water-soluble fraction spills into urine
No bilirubin reaches colonic bacteria
Urobilinogen and stercobilin fall, stools turn pale

idea.rule: Obstructive jaundice: conjugated bilirubin up, urine bilirubin present, urobilinogen and stercobilin gone.
also: Hemolysis: unconjugated up, urine urobilinogen up, no urine bilirubin
Gilbert syndrome: unconjugated up only, urine normal
Pancreatic head cancer and choledocholithiasis give the same obstructive pattern
Alkaline phosphatase and GGT rise with the conjugated bilirubin

stem: In an anesthetized animal, a loop of jejunum is isolated and a labeled dipeptide is placed in its lumen. Over 30 minutes the label left in the lumen is mostly intact dipeptide, intestinal lymph carries almost no label, and portal blood sampled before the liver carries labeled free amino acids. The same dipeptide injected straight into portal blood stays intact.
oneliner: Experiment + labeled dipeptide in jejunal loop + luminal label intact + free amino acids in portal blood + dipeptide stable in blood → where split?
ask: Where was the dipeptide mainly hydrolyzed to free amino acids?

whyNot.A: The label left in the lumen is **mostly intact dipeptide**, so little splitting happens there
whyNot.B: Dipeptide injected **straight into portal blood stays intact**, so blood is not where it is split
whyNot.C: Portal blood **sampled before the liver** already holds free amino acids
whyNot.D: Intestinal lymph carries **almost no label**; amino acids leave by portal blood

answer: Jejunal enterocytes (brush border and cytoplasmic peptidases)
why: Pancreatic and gastric proteases break protein into **small peptides** in the lumen. **Di- and tripeptides** are then taken up by the **H+-coupled transporter PepT1** and split to free amino acids by **peptidases in the brush border and enterocyte cytoplasm**, so the portal blood gets amino acids.
chain: Pancreatic proteases make oligopeptides in the lumen
PepT1 carries di- and tripeptides into enterocytes
Cytoplasmic peptidases release free amino acids
Amino acids exit the basolateral membrane
Portal blood carries free amino acids to the liver

idea.rule: Proteins are split to oligopeptides in the lumen; di- and tripeptides are finished inside the enterocyte.
also: Hartnup disease: neutral amino acids are still absorbed as di- and tripeptides via PepT1
Cystinuria: dibasic amino acids are still absorbed in peptide form
Disaccharides are likewise finished at the brush border, not in the lumen

stem: A 45-year-old man is seen one week after emergency surgery for appendicitis, during which he ate little for a few days. He feels well. His sclerae look mildly yellow, his urine and stools are normal in color, and the abdomen shows only a healing wound. Hemoglobin is 14.1 g/dL.
oneliner: 45M + 1 week after surgery + poor intake + mild scleral icterus + normal urine and stool color + Hb 14.1 → bilirubin fractions, AST/ALT, urine bilirubin, Hb?
ask: Which set of laboratory results is expected?

options.A: Unconjugated ↑, conjugated ↑, AST/ALT ↔, urine bilirubin ↑, hemoglobin ↔
options.B: Unconjugated ↑, conjugated ↔, AST/ALT ↑↑, urine bilirubin ↔, hemoglobin ↔
options.C: Unconjugated ↑, conjugated ↔, AST/ALT ↔, urine bilirubin ↔, hemoglobin ↔
options.D: Unconjugated ↑, conjugated ↔, AST/ALT ↔, urine bilirubin ↔, hemoglobin ↓
options.E: Unconjugated ↑, conjugated ↔, AST/ALT ↔, urine bilirubin ↑, hemoglobin ↔

whyNot.A: A raised conjugated fraction spills into urine and darkens it; his **urine is normal in color**
whyNot.B: Marked transaminase elevation means hepatocyte injury; he **feels well and has no abdominal findings** apart from the wound
whyNot.D: Hemolysis would lower hemoglobin; his is **14.1 g/dL**
whyNot.E: Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and does not reach urine, and bilirubin in urine would darken it; his **urine is normal in color**

answer: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with otherwise normal tests
why: Reduced **UGT1A1** activity (Gilbert syndrome) leaves only a small reserve for conjugation, so **fasting, illness or surgery** pushes **unconjugated** bilirubin up. The conjugated fraction, **aminotransferases and hemoglobin stay normal** and no bilirubin appears in urine because the unconjugated form is albumin-bound.
chain: Baseline UGT1A1 activity is reduced
Fasting and surgery add stress on conjugation
Unconjugated bilirubin accumulates
Conjugated fraction is unaffected
Liver enzymes and hemoglobin stay normal

idea.rule: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver tests and no hemolysis, brought out by stress, means Gilbert.
also: Fasting, dehydration and febrile illness raise bilirubin transiently
Crigler-Najjar has complete or severe UGT1A1 loss
Dubin-Johnson and Rotor raise conjugated bilirubin
Hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin but lowers hemoglobin and haptoglobin

stem: A 62-year-old man has taken a proton pump inhibitor daily for 6 weeks for epigastric burning that eases with meals. He has no weight loss, diarrhea or vomiting. Fasting gastric pH, antral somatostatin and serum gastrin are measured.
oneliner: 62M + daily PPI for 6 weeks + meal-relieved epigastric pain → gastric pH, antral somatostatin, serum gastrin?
ask: Which set of changes is expected?

whyNot.B: Somatostatin release is driven by **acid**; with acid blocked by the PPI it cannot rise, and gastrin would not fall
whyNot.C: The **PPI blocks the H+/K+ ATPase**, so gastric pH cannot fall
whyNot.D: Raised pH removes the **brake on G cells**, so gastrin cannot stay unchanged
whyNot.E: A PPI **raises** pH, so a fall in pH is the wrong direction for both

answer: pH up, somatostatin down, gastrin up
why: The PPI **blocks the proton pump**, so gastric **pH rises**. Less acid means **less somatostatin from antral D cells**, which removes inhibition of **G cells**, and **gastrin rises**. This is why a gastrin level must be interpreted with gastric pH or off the PPI.
chain: PPI inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase
Gastric pH rises
D cells release less somatostatin
G cells lose inhibition
Serum gastrin rises

idea.rule: Acid and somatostatin brake gastrin; lose the acid and gastrin rises.
also: Atrophic gastritis: high pH and high gastrin
Zollinger-Ellison: high gastrin with low pH, so no feedback
H2 blockers raise gastrin to a lesser degree
Long-term PPI use can cause rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping

stem: Bile is sampled from the hepatic duct and from the gallbladder of the same fasted volunteer, and the share of the bile made up by each constituent is compared between the two samples.
oneliner: Experiment + hepatic bile vs gallbladder bile from same fasted subject → which constituent's proportion is lower?
ask: The proportion of which constituent is lower in gallbladder bile than in hepatic bile?

whyNot.A: Bile salts stay behind as **water is removed**, so their concentration rises
whyNot.D: Cholesterol is **retained**, so its concentration climbs along with that of the bile salts
whyNot.E: Calcium is **left behind** as fluid is absorbed, and a higher concentration favours stone formation

why: The gallbladder mucosa absorbs **Na+, Cl- and water isosmotically**, so stored bile is concentrated several-fold. **Water falls** in proportion, while **bile salts, bilirubin, cholesterol and calcium** all become more concentrated.
chain: Gallbladder mucosa absorbs Na+ and Cl-
Water follows isosmotically
Fluid volume falls during fasting
Bile salts, cholesterol and bilirubin concentrate
Bile reaches the duodenum concentrated after CCK

idea.rule: Gallbladder concentrates bile by absorbing salt and water; solutes stay behind.
also: Over-concentration and stasis promote gallstones
CCK empties the concentrated bile into the duodenum
Bile is also acidified in the gallbladder as bicarbonate is absorbed
The colon likewise absorbs Na+ and water, concentrating what is left in stool

stem: A 58-year-old man with 25 years of heavy alcohol use has ascites, spider angiomata and esophageal varices. Ultrasound shows a coarse, nodular liver with patent portal and hepatic veins, and echocardiography is normal. During hepatic vein catheterization, pressures are recorded in the portal vein, the wedged hepatic vein, the free hepatic vein and the right atrium.
oneliner: 58M + heavy alcohol + ascites, varices, spider angiomata + nodular liver, patent veins, normal echo → portal, wedged hepatic, free hepatic, RA pressures?
ask: Which set of pressures is expected?

options.A: Portal ↑, wedged hepatic ↔, free hepatic ↔, RA ↔
options.B: Portal ↑, wedged hepatic ↑, free hepatic ↔, RA ↔
options.C: Portal ↑, wedged hepatic ↑, free hepatic ↑, RA ↔
options.D: Portal ↑, wedged hepatic ↑, free hepatic ↑, RA ↑
options.E: Portal ↔, wedged hepatic ↔, free hepatic ↔, RA ↔

whyNot.A: A normal wedge with a high portal pressure is a **presinusoidal** block (portal vein thrombosis, schistosomiasis); his **portal vein is patent** and the liver is scarred
whyNot.C: A raised free hepatic pressure means a block **downstream** of the sinusoids (hepatic vein or IVC thrombosis); his **hepatic veins are patent**
whyNot.D: All four rising is **right heart failure**; his **echocardiogram is normal**
whyNot.E: He has **ascites and varices**, which need raised portal pressure

answer: Portal and wedged hepatic pressures up; free hepatic and right atrial pressures unchanged (sinusoidal portal hypertension)
why: Scarring and regenerative nodules block flow at the **sinusoids**. The **wedged hepatic pressure** reflects sinusoidal pressure, so it climbs with the portal pressure, while the **free hepatic vein** and **right atrium** lie beyond the block and stay normal. The wedged minus free gap is the hepatic venous pressure gradient.
chain: Fibrosis and nodules narrow and collapse the sinusoids
Resistance to flow through the liver rises
Portal pressure rises, giving varices and ascites
Wedged hepatic pressure samples sinusoidal pressure, so it rises with it
Free hepatic vein and right atrium lie beyond the block, so they stay normal

idea.rule: Wedged minus free hepatic pressure shows a sinusoidal block; free hepatic and RA pressures stay normal.
also: Portal vein thrombosis or schistosomiasis (presinusoidal): portal pressure up, wedged pressure normal
Budd-Chiari syndrome (postsinusoidal): free and wedged hepatic pressures rise as well
Right heart failure raises all four pressures, including the RA
A hepatic venous pressure gradient of 10 mmHg or more is clinically significant portal hypertension

stem: A 30-year-old woman has burning behind the breastbone that begins within an hour of large fried meals and rarely follows small low-fat meals. Antacids give only brief relief. She has no trouble swallowing, no weight loss and no bleeding, does not smoke or drink alcohol, and takes no medications.
oneliner: 30F + heartburn after large fried meals + antacids brief relief + no alarm features → hormone and LES pressure change after fat?
ask: Which hormone change and which change in lower esophageal sphincter (LES) pressure follow a fatty meal?

whyNot.A: Gastrin is driven by **protein and stretch**, not fat, and a higher LES pressure would **hold reflux back**
whyNot.B: Secretin is released by **duodenal acid**, and a rise in LES pressure would not explain **meal-triggered reflux**
whyNot.C: Motilin peaks **between meals**, not after a fatty one, and a tighter LES would not cause her burning
whyNot.E: Somatostatin is a broad **inhibitory** hormone, not the fat signal that loosens the LES, and an **unchanged LES** would not explain burning after large fatty meals

answer: CCK rises and LES pressure falls
why: Fat and fatty acids in the duodenum release **CCK**, which **lowers LES pressure** (gastrin raises it) and **slows gastric emptying**. The sphincter is looser and the stomach stays full longer, so reflux worsens after **large fatty meals**.
chain: Fat and fatty acids reach the duodenum
I cells release CCK
CCK lowers LES pressure
CCK slows gastric emptying, so the stomach stays full
More gastric content refluxes after large fatty meals

idea.rule: Fat in the duodenum releases CCK, which relaxes the LES and delays gastric emptying.
also: Gastrin raises LES pressure, so protein-triggered gastrin does not cause reflux this way
CCK also contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi
Chocolate, caffeine and peppermint also lower LES pressure
Because CCK slows gastric emptying, a fatty meal stays in the stomach longer and keeps reflux going

stem: A 32-year-old woman leaks stool when she coughs and cannot hold gas since a long labor ending in a forceps vaginal delivery four years ago. Her neurologic examination is normal and she has no diabetes or bowel disease. Endoanal ultrasound shows an anterior gap through both the inner and outer sphincter rings. Anorectal manometry is performed.
oneliner: 32F + leaks stool and gas since forceps delivery + normal neuro exam + gap in both sphincter rings → resting and squeeze pressures?
ask: Which pair of resting and squeeze anal pressures is expected?

whyNot.B: High pressures mean a **spastic** sphincter, which gives pain or constipation, and **ultrasound shows a tear**
whyNot.C: A high resting pressure with normal squeeze is an **internal sphincter that will not relax**; a **torn** ring cannot raise tone
whyNot.D: Low resting with preserved squeeze is an **internal-only** injury; her **outer ring is torn** too
whyNot.E: Normal tone with strong squeeze would keep her **continent**, but she **leaks**

answer: Resting and squeeze anal pressures both reduced
why: The **internal sphincter** (smooth muscle) provides most **resting tone**, and the **external sphincter** (skeletal muscle, pudendal nerve) provides **voluntary squeeze**. A tear through both rings lowers both pressures, so the canal cannot stay closed against rectal contents.
chain: Delivery tears the anterior sphincter complex
Internal sphincter smooth muscle is disrupted, so resting tone falls
External sphincter skeletal muscle is disrupted, so squeeze falls
The canal cannot close against rectal pressure
Leakage of gas and stool follows

idea.rule: Resting tone is the internal sphincter (smooth muscle); squeeze is the external sphincter (skeletal muscle).
also: Pudendal neuropathy from childbirth lowers squeeze more than resting pressure
Spinal cord or cauda equina injury lowers squeeze pressure
In Hirschsprung disease the internal sphincter fails to relax when the rectum is stretched
Spastic puborectalis or sphincter gives constipation, not leakage

stem: A 3-month-old boy has had watery, acidic diarrhea since the first weeks of life and weighs below the 3rd percentile. He is mildly dehydrated and his stool is positive for reducing substances. A cousin had the same illness in infancy. After an oral glucose load his blood glucose does not rise, but it rises normally after an oral fructose load.
oneliner: 3-month-old boy + watery acidic diarrhea since infancy + stool reducing substances + flat glucose load, normal fructose load + affected cousin → defective transporter?
ask: Which intestinal protein is most likely defective?

whyNot.A: GLUT5 carries **fructose**, and he absorbs a fructose load **normally**
whyNot.B: GLUT4 is the insulin-responsive carrier of **muscle and fat**, not of the intestinal brush border
whyNot.C: Lactase splits **lactose**; a **glucose load** is already a monosaccharide and would still be absorbed
whyNot.D: It cleaves **sucrose and maltose**; an oral glucose load bypasses it

why: Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes through **Na⁺-coupled SGLT1**, whereas fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through **GLUT5**. Without SGLT1 the sugars stay in the lumen, hold water and are fermented to acid, giving **osmotic, acidic diarrhea**, while **fructose absorption is normal**.
chain: SGLT1 is absent from the brush border
Glucose and galactose are not absorbed in the small intestine
Blood glucose does not rise after oral glucose
Unabsorbed sugar holds water and is fermented by colonic bacteria to acid
Watery, acidic stool with reducing substances results
Fructose uses GLUT5, so its absorption is unchanged

idea.rule: Glucose and galactose need SGLT1 (Na⁺ coupled); fructose uses GLUT5.
also: Lactase or sucrase-isomaltase deficiency spares a glucose load because the sugar is already a monosaccharide
Defective basolateral GLUT2 causes Fanconi-Bickel syndrome
Unabsorbed sugar gives an osmotic diarrhea that stops with fasting
Fermentation of unabsorbed sugar makes stool acidic and positive for reducing substances

stem: In an experiment, gastric fluid is aspirated from a breast-fed 2-week-old infant 30 minutes after a feed, and lipase activity is measured at the aspirate's acid pH. Pancreatic lipase output is still low at this age. The aspirate contains four times more free fatty acids than the milk that was fed.
oneliner: Breast-fed 2-week-old + gastric aspirate after feed + low pancreatic lipase + free fatty acids 4× the milk → lipase substrate?
ask: Which dietary component is the lipase in the aspirate acting on?

whyNot.A: Cholesterol is **not a lipase substrate**; ester hydrolysis needs pancreatic cholesterol esterase, which is **low** at this age
whyNot.B: Retinyl esters are a **trace** fraction of milk fat and need **pancreatic** esterases, which are **low** at this age; they could not raise free fatty acids **fourfold**
whyNot.D: Free fatty acids are the **product**, and they are what **rose** in the aspirate
whyNot.E: Phospholipids are cleaved by **pancreatic phospholipase A2**, which is also **low** at this age

shifts.var: Free fatty acids in gastric contents

why: Breast-milk fat is mostly **triglyceride**. With **pancreatic lipase low** in a newborn, **lingual and gastric lipase** (with milk lipase) start the job in the stomach, working at acid pH and releasing **free fatty acids** before the duodenum.
chain: Milk fat arrives as triglyceride
Pancreatic lipase output is low in the newborn
Lingual and gastric lipase act in the acid stomach
Triglyceride is cut to free fatty acids and diglycerides
Free fatty acids in the gastric fluid rise

idea.rule: Lipases hydrolyze triglycerides; in newborns lingual and gastric lipase cover for low pancreatic lipase.
also: Lingual lipase keeps working at gastric pH
Pancreatic lipase needs colipase and bile salt micelles
In cystic fibrosis, pancreatic insufficiency causes fat malabsorption
Medium-chain triglycerides need less bile and pancreatic lipase
